title: Real-Time Transport
summary: How a server tells a client something happened, when HTTP was designed for the client to do all the asking. The answer evolves — short polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets — and each step exists because the previous one broke under a specific load.
analogy: Ringing the post office every five minutes to ask whether post has arrived. Most calls are wasted, so instead you stay on the line and they speak when something comes — but now the line is held open, and if either of you says nothing for a while someone hangs up assuming the other left. Keeping the line open is cheaper than calling constantly, right up until ten thousand people are holding lines and the switchboard has to remember which operator each of them is talking to.

explanation.beginner: Normal web requests only go one way to start with: the browser asks, the server answers, and the connection closes. That is fine for loading a page, but it means the server has no way to say 'a new message arrived' on its own. The oldest fix is to ask over and over — polling. A better fix is to ask once and let the server hold the question until it has an answer. Better still, the server can keep a one-way stream open and push updates down it. A WebSocket goes furthest: it starts as a normal HTTP request, then both sides agree to upgrade the same connection into a two-way channel that stays open, and either side can send at any time.
explanation.interview: Four transports, each one solving the previous one's failure. Short polling: a request on a fixed interval; simple and stateless, but cost scales with clients divided by interval regardless of whether anything changed, and latency is bounded below by that interval. Long polling: the server holds the request until data exists or a timeout fires; latency drops to near-zero but every waiting client still occupies a connection, and every message costs a full request/response cycle with headers. Server-Sent Events: one long-lived HTTP response streaming text frames, with automatic reconnect and Last-Event-ID replay built into the browser — but it is server-to-client only and, over HTTP/1.1, competes for the roughly six connections per origin a browser allows. WebSockets: an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket and Sec-WebSocket-Key, answered with 101 Switching Protocols, after which the same TCP connection carries framed binary or text in both directions with 2–14 bytes of framing rather than hundreds of bytes of headers. The cost is statefulness: a connection lives on one server process, so delivery requires sticky routing or a pub/sub backplane to fan a message to whichever node holds the recipient; load balancer idle timeouts terminate quiet connections, so you need application-level pings; and every drop needs reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter and a cursor-based replay so messages sent during the gap are not lost.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.note: Opens one connection and keeps it. Must reconnect with backoff and ask for anything missed while it was gone.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.note: Must pass the Upgrade handshake through, and its idle timeout — commonly 60 s — will close a quiet connection unless heartbeats keep it warm.

nodes.label: WS server A
nodes.note: Holds this user's live connection in memory. That state is why the routing problem exists.

without: At a 5-second poll interval, 100,000 clients generate 20,000 requests/s that are almost all empty
Every one of those carries full HTTP headers — hundreds of bytes to say 'nothing new'
A change still waits up to a full interval before anyone sees it
with: One open connection per client; frames cost 2–14 bytes of overhead
Delivery latency is one network trip, not one poll interval
Traffic scales with events, not with clients times polling frequency
why.conclusion: You trade a stateless, trivially scalable request pattern for a stateful connection that pins a user to a process — and everything hard about WebSockets follows from that one sentence.

nodes.label: WS server B
nodes.note: Holds a different set of connections. It has no idea who is connected to server A.

nodes.label: Pub/sub backplane
nodes.note: Every node subscribes to the channels its connected users care about, so a publisher does not need to know which node holds whom.

nodes.label: App / worker
nodes.note: Publishes an event once. Fan-out to the right connections is the backplane's job, not the publisher's.

without: The server can never speak first, so anything it learns waits until the client next asks
Short polling at a 5-second interval with 100,000 connected clients is 20,000 requests/s, and on a quiet day essentially all of them return nothing
Each empty poll still carries request and response headers — commonly several hundred bytes each way to communicate 'no change'
Lowering the interval to improve freshness multiplies the wasted traffic linearly; you are buying latency with load
with: One connection carries many messages; per-message overhead falls from hundreds of bytes to a 2–14 byte frame header
Delivery latency is a single network trip after the event happens, not up to one polling interval
Traffic volume tracks how much actually happens rather than how many clients exist times how often they ask
The channel is bidirectional, so client-originated events (typing indicators, cursor positions, acknowledgements) ride the same connection
why.conclusion: Real-time transport is a ladder, and you should climb only as far as the problem forces you. Each rung buys latency and efficiency and pays for it in connection state — and connection state is what turns a simple stateless service into one that needs sticky routing, heartbeats, a backplane and a replay story.

whenToUse: Updates are frequent and their freshness is the product — chat, collaborative editing, live presence, trading or telemetry dashboards
Both directions matter: the client sends as well as receives, and you would otherwise need a socket plus a separate POST path
Sub-second delivery is a requirement you would have to defend, not a nice-to-have
Many small messages, where per-message HTTP header overhead would dominate the payload
Many clients care about the same event, so one publish fans out rather than each client polling independently
whenNotToUse: Updates are infrequent — a handful of events per user per hour. You would hold an idle connection, a heartbeat timer and a slot in a routing table for hours to deliver almost nothing; polling every 30 seconds is cheaper and cannot break in a way that needs a reconnection strategy

The client only ever sends, never receives — form submissions, event ingestion, analytics beacons. A plain HTTP POST is simpler, retries cleanly, needs no connection state and works through every proxy you will ever meet

The server only ever sends, never receives, and the payload is text — Server-Sent Events gives you that with automatic browser reconnect and Last-Event-ID replay for free, and none of the WebSocket routing problems

The data is a request/response question with an answer ('what is this user's profile?'). Wrapping request/response in a persistent socket means rebuilding correlation ids, timeouts and error semantics that HTTP already has

Corporate proxies or network middleboxes in your client population strip or mishandle the Upgrade handshake, and you have no fallback path — you have traded a working slow system for a broken fast one

pros: Trivially simple; ordinary stateless HTTP requests that any client, proxy and load balancer already handles
No connection state, so any server can answer any request and scaling is just adding servers
Fails gracefully — a missed poll is corrected by the next one
cons: Cost is clients divided by interval, independent of how much actually changes: 100,000 clients at 5 s is 20,000 req/s of mostly empty responses
Latency is bounded below by the interval, so freshness can only be bought with proportionally more load
Header overhead dwarfs the payload when the answer is 'nothing new'

pros: Near-real-time delivery using nothing but ordinary HTTP requests
Works through essentially every proxy and firewall, because it looks like a slow response
No protocol upgrade, so existing routing, auth and logging all still apply unchanged
cons: A held request still occupies a connection and, on thread-per-request servers, a thread — the resource saving over polling is smaller than it looks
Every delivered message costs a full request/response cycle plus a reconnect, so under heavy traffic it degrades toward the cost of polling
A race window exists between the response returning and the next request being issued, so the server must buffer or the client must send a cursor

pros: One long-lived HTTP response streaming events; no upgrade, no new protocol, plain text frames
Automatic reconnection and Last-Event-ID replay are built into the browser, so the hardest part of real-time is handled for you
Still ordinary HTTP, so compression, auth headers and existing proxy configuration keep working
cons: One direction only — anything the client wants to send needs a separate request path
Text only; binary payloads must be encoded, costing roughly a third more bytes in base64
Over HTTP/1.1 it consumes one of the browser's roughly six connections per origin, which several open tabs will exhaust — HTTP/2 multiplexing removes this, but only if every hop speaks it

pros: Full duplex over one connection: either side sends at any time with 2–14 bytes of framing
Lowest per-message overhead and lowest delivery latency of the four
Carries binary natively, and one connection serves every channel a client subscribes to
cons: Stateful: a connection lives on one process, so you need sticky routing or a pub/sub backplane before a second server exists
Load balancer and proxy idle timeouts close quiet connections, so you must implement pings and reconnect with backoff and jitter — otherwise every restart produces a synchronised reconnect storm
You inherit responsibilities HTTP handled: message ordering, acknowledgement, replay of anything sent during a disconnect, and per-connection auth expiry
Idle connections are not free — each costs kernel socket buffers plus application state, so capacity planning becomes memory and file descriptors rather than requests per second

keyNumbers.label: Short polling cost: 100,000 clients at a 5 s interval
Per-message overhead: HTTP headers vs WebSocket frame
Memory per idle WebSocket connection
keyNumbers.value: ~10–50 KB, socket buffers plus application state

keyNumbers.label: Common load balancer idle timeout
keyNumbers.value: 60 s — heartbeat well inside it, typically every 20–30 s

keyNumbers.label: Browser connection limit per origin over HTTP/1.1
keyNumbers.value: about 6, which caps concurrent SSE streams

keyNumbers.label: Handshake response that switches protocols
keyNumbers.value: HTTP 101 Switching Protocols, on the same TCP connection

quiz.question: Your chat service works perfectly on one server. You add a second server behind a load balancer and users start missing messages: Alice on server A sends to Bob, who is connected to server B, and nothing arrives. What broke and what is the standard fix?
options: The load balancer is not passing the Upgrade header; enable WebSocket support on it

A WebSocket connection is state held in one process, so server A has no way to reach a socket owned by server B. Publish the message to a pub/sub backplane that every node subscribes to, so whichever node holds Bob delivers it
TLS is being terminated twice; terminate it only at the load balancer
Bob's client needs to poll as well as hold the socket, to catch messages the socket missed
quiz.explanation: This is the single consequence that makes WebSockets harder than HTTP. A stateless HTTP request can be answered by any server, so horizontal scaling is free; a live socket exists in exactly one process's memory, so the sender's server must somehow reach the recipient's. Sticky routing does not solve it either — it keeps a client pinned to a server, which is necessary, but says nothing about how a message crosses between servers. The backplane (Redis pub/sub, a message broker, or a dedicated routing tier) is what decouples 'who publishes' from 'who holds the connection'. Note the second half of the problem too: Bob may be offline entirely, so durable storage plus replay on reconnect is still required.

quiz.question: A dashboard streams server-to-client metric updates as JSON, and the client never needs to send anything over the same channel. Which transport is the best fit and why?
options: WebSockets, because they are the lowest-latency option available
Server-Sent Events, because it is one-directional text streaming and the browser gives you automatic reconnection and Last-Event-ID replay for free
Short polling, because dashboards do not need real-time data
Long polling, because it is the only option that works through corporate proxies
quiz.explanation: Picking the most capable transport is not the same as picking the right one. SSE is plain HTTP, so your existing auth, compression and proxy configuration keep working, and the two hardest parts of any real-time client — reconnecting sensibly and not losing events during the gap — are implemented in the browser rather than by you. Choosing WebSockets here means writing your own reconnect, backoff, heartbeat and replay logic to gain a duplex channel you will never use in one direction. The honest limits of SSE are text-only payloads and the roughly six-connection-per-origin cap on HTTP/1.1, and neither bites a single dashboard tab.

quiz.question: Connections to your WebSocket service drop reliably after about a minute of inactivity, and when they do, clients reconnect instantly and in unison, briefly overwhelming the service. Name both causes.
options: TCP keepalive is disabled, and the client retry loop is too slow

An idle timeout at the load balancer or proxy closes quiet connections — fix with application-level pings inside that window — and reconnecting without exponential backoff and jitter synchronises every client into a thundering herd
The server is running out of file descriptors, and the clients are caching the old address
The Upgrade handshake is expiring and must be re-sent periodically
quiz.explanation: Two separate bugs that always appear together. Intermediaries close connections that carry no bytes — 60 seconds is a common default — and TCP keepalive usually does not help because its defaults are measured in hours and middleboxes may ignore it anyway; an application-level ping every 20–30 seconds does. The second bug is the reconnect: if every client retries immediately, a single blip re-establishes tens of thousands of connections in the same instant, which is exactly the load the service is least able to absorb while recovering. Exponential backoff with random jitter spreads them out, and the reconnect should carry a cursor or last-received id so the server can replay what was missed rather than leaving a silent gap.
